1331.title: Gimel runs to dalet (Shabbat 104a)
1331.hook: the rabbis say gimel's foot runs after dalet: the giver chases the poor
1331.howItsDone: Jewish teaching on tzedakah, giving to those in need, prizes giving that seeks out the need and spares the receiver shame; the Talmud reads this into the shapes of gimel and dalet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bet: closed on three sides, open toward what comes next. Your line: bet is a house. Today, the third and fourth letters, and what they do together.

The Talmud tells of a classroom turned upside down. Some young children walk into the house of study, where the rabbis sit with their books, and start teaching. Not reciting. Teaching. They go through the alphabet letter by letter, explaining what each one is saying, and the rabbis write it down, impressed enough to say nothing like it had been heard in a very long time. At the third and fourth letters, gimel and dalet, the children point at something tiny in how the letters are drawn. A foot.
screen: `CHILDREN IN THE HOUSE OF STUDY.` → `THEY TEACH THE RABBIS.` → `GIMEL, DALET, AND A FOOT.`

segments.voice: First, the two letters as a phrase. The children read gimel dalet as gemol dalim: be kind to the poor. Gimel stands for the giver, dalet for the one in need. Second, the foot. Gimel is drawn with a little leg reaching out at the bottom, toward dalet. Why? Because, the children say, it's the way of someone who does kindness to run after the poor. Not to sit at home and wait for a knock. To go looking. Third, dalet's answer. Dalet has a leg of its own, reaching back toward gimel, so the poor person makes themselves available to be found. But dalet's face is turned away from gimel, so the gift is given in secret, and the one receiving it isn't ashamed. Run toward the need, then look away while it's met. Fourth, the giving itself. Giving only when asked, or only when seen, asks little. These two letters ask something harder: notice the need before anyone has to say it, close the distance yourself, and protect the other person's dignity, so what they remember is the help, not the embarrassment. The children in the study house found all of that in a foot and a turned face. Tomorrow, dalet.

If you pray, hold that person in your prayer.

1332.title: Dalet
1332.hook: delet is a door; dal means poor
1332.howItsDone: Children learning the Hebrew alphabet are often taught dalet alongside delet, door; and the Talmud's reading of gimel and dalet as 'be kind to the poor' is a teaching some families and schools share when they talk about giving in secret.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gimel's foot reaching toward the next letter. Your line: gimel runs to dalet. Today, the letter being chased.

A door has two sides, and it matters which one you're on. From inside, a door is warmth, privacy, a lock at night. From outside, it's a question: will anyone open? Today's letter is drawn with two strokes, a line across the top and a line down the right side, meeting at a corner like a doorframe seen from the edge. Say its name slowly: dalet. Now say the Hebrew word for a door: delet. Almost the same sound. And the rabbis heard a third word hiding nearby.
screen: `TWO SIDES OF A DOOR.` → `TWO STROKES, ONE CORNER.` → `DALET, DELET.`

segments.voice: First, the door. Delet is the ordinary Hebrew word for a door on hinges, and the letter's name sounds just like it. Whether one comes from the other is a question for the language scholars; for a learner, it's a handle. See dalet, see a door. Second, the poor. In Hebrew, dal means someone poor, someone thin, someone low. The Torah uses it in its laws: when a person who is dal brings an offering, the law makes room for a smaller one, so being poor never shuts anyone out. Third, a door with no hinges. In Psalm one hundred forty-one, the poet asks for help with speech. In the King James: "Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips." The Hebrew word for door there is dal, the same short word that elsewhere means poor. The mouth has a door too, and it needs a guard. Yesterday the Talmud read gimel and dalet as be kind to the poor; the psalm adds: watch what comes through the door of your lips while you're kind. Fourth, today. Need arrives at doors: the neighbor who knocks to borrow something, the new person at the edge of the room, the friend who texts, deletes, then texts again. Dalet asks two things at once: open the door of the house, and guard the door of the mouth, so nobody leaves smaller than they came.

1333.title: Heh
1333.hook: the breath sound, added to Abram and Sarai to make Abraham and Sarah
1333.howItsDone: Children learning the alef-bet may be taught heh by its soft h sound; the renaming of Abram and Sarai in Genesis 17 is read in synagogue as part of the cycle of Torah readings, and some teachers point out the added heh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a letter that sounds like a door and sits beside the word for poor. Your line: dalet is a door. Today, a letter that's almost nothing but air.

"Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham." That's God speaking in Genesis, to a man already old who has been Abram all his life. Later in the same chapter it happens again, to his wife: no more Sarai, from now on Sarah. Two new names, in a single conversation. In English it looks like a few letters shuffled. In Hebrew the change is smaller, and stranger: each name gains the same letter, one that barely makes a sound. It's the letter you'd use to write a sigh.
screen: `ABRAM BECOMES ABRAHAM.` → `SARAI BECOMES SARAH.` → `ONE LETTER, NEARLY SILENT.`

segments.voice: First, the sound. Say it with your hand in front of your mouth: heh. No tongue, no lips, no teeth, just warm air, about as close as speech comes to simply breathing out. Second, Abram. In Hebrew his name gains a heh in the middle and becomes Avraham, and the verse gives the reason in the same breath: "for the father of a multitude of nations have I made thee." A promise, sealed by adding a breath. Third, Sarai. Her change works differently: the yud at the end comes off, and a heh takes its place. "As for Sarai thy wife, thou shalt not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall her name be." Husband and wife both carry the same new letter out of that conversation. Why heh? Some answer that it's the letter of breath, and a new name is like a new breath of life. Some rabbis go further. In the Talmud, in tractate Menachot, they take a word from Genesis about the heavens and the earth being created and split it in two: be-heh, with heh, and bera'am, he created them. This world, they read, was made with the breath letter. Fourth, what it means for a person. Abraham and Sarah didn't get new faces or new families that day. They got one breath added to who they already were. Not a new person. The same person, with a little more air in them.

Do it again, letting the breath out be longer than the breath in, and if a name comes to mind, yours or someone you love, let it ride on the breath. If you pray, let the breath be a prayer without words.

1334.title: Vav
1334.hook: a hook, and the word "and": it joins things
1334.howItsDone: Children learning Hebrew may meet vav early, both as a letter and as the prefix ve-, 'and'; readers of the Hebrew Bible hear it at the start of verse after verse in the stories of Genesis.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a breath added to two names: Abram became Abraham, Sarai became Sarah. Your line: heh is breath. Today, a letter that holds things together.

In Exodus, Moses is given building plans for the Tabernacle, the tent where God's presence would dwell among the people. The list is detailed: boards, sockets, curtains of blue and purple and scarlet. And somewhere in it, a tiny, practical part. Something has to hold the curtain up. The pillars get hooks of gold. Nobody comes to see the hooks. But without them a beautiful curtain is a heap of cloth on the floor. The Hebrew word for those hooks is the name of today's letter.
screen: `BUILDING THE TABERNACLE.` → `CURTAINS OF BLUE AND SCARLET.` → `HOOKS OF GOLD.`

segments.voice: Three things hang on this little hook. First, the word. In the Tabernacle instructions, the hooks on the pillars are vavim, the plural of vav. The King James puts it plainly: "their hooks shall be of gold." The letter looks the part: a single upright stroke with a small bend at the top, like a peg on a wall. Second, a job. In Hebrew, "and" isn't a separate word. It's this letter, clipped onto the front of the next word: ve. Hooked on. Open Genesis in Hebrew and watch it work, sentence after sentence. The King James keeps many of the hooks: "And God said, Let there be light: and there was light." Each part of creation is fastened to the one before, and the story never lets go of the thread. Third, a surprise. Sometimes vav stops being a consonant and carries a vowel, an o or an oo. In shalom, the o you hear in the middle is held up by a vav. The letter that joins sentences also joins sounds. That's vav's whole character: rarely the point of the sentence, and the sentence falls apart without it. A lot of good work looks like that. The person who introduces two friends. The text that says, I'll come with you. A small and that keeps two things from falling apart.

Don't fix anything yet; just let the word and sit between them, this and that, and feel what it would take to hook them together. If you pray, bring both into your prayer at once.

1335.title: Zayin
1335.hook: the letter that begins zachor, remember
1335.howItsDone: Congregations welcome the Sabbath on Friday evening by singing Lecha Dodi, whose verses include the teaching that 'keep' and 'remember' were spoken as one; the kiddush over wine on Friday night also speaks of the Sabbath as a remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hook of gold and the little letter that means and. Your line: vav connects. Today, a letter that reaches backward.

A puzzle hiding in plain sight. The Ten Commandments appear in Exodus, and then again, when Moses retells them, in Deuteronomy. Side by side, they're nearly the same. But the Sabbath commandment opens with a different word in each. In Exodus it's zachor: remember. In Deuteronomy, it's shamor: keep, guard, observe. Which one did the people hear at the mountain? The rabbis had an answer, and you can still hear it sung on Friday nights.

First, the word it opens. Zachor, remember. In the King James: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." The very first sound of that command is a zayin. So is the first sound of zikaron, a memory, and zecher, a remembrance. Second, the other word. Deuteronomy opens with shamor, to guard or observe. Remember is something you do inside. Guard is something you do with your hands and your calendar. Two verbs, one day. Third, the rabbis' answer. In the Talmud, in tractate Shevuot, they say God spoke both words at once, in a single utterance, something no human mouth could do. Much later, a poet put that teaching into Lecha Dodi, the song congregations sing on Friday evening to welcome the Sabbath. One of its lines says it outright: keep and remember, in one word. The puzzle became a song. Fourth, why remembering gets its own commandment. In this tradition, memory isn't just what happens to you. It's something you do on purpose. The prayer for the dead said on certain festivals is called Yizkor, may God remember. Zayin turns the past into a task: not waiting for a memory to arrive, but choosing to call someone to mind.

segments.voice: Choose something to remember instead of waiting for it to drift in: a person who taught you something, a morning when things went right, a kindness someone did for you and has probably forgotten. Bring it back slowly, where you were, what it sounded like, what they said, and stay with each detail as it arrives. If you pray, hold that memory in your prayer.

1336.title: Chet
1336.hook: with yud it spells chai, life
1336.howItsDone: At Jewish celebrations, from weddings to a meal after a hard day, people raise a glass and say l'chaim, 'to life'; some give gifts in multiples of eighteen, the number tradition assigns to chai, and some wear the word chai as a pendant.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two words for the Sabbath, remember and keep, spoken as one. Your line: zayin remembers. Today, a letter you may already have heard at a party.

The speeches are over. Somebody's uncle talked a little too long, the bride's friend made everyone cry, and now the glasses go up: wine, whiskey, sparkling water, whatever's in hand. The whole table says one word together: l'chaim! Glasses touch. At Jewish weddings, at a bris, at a new job, even after a funeral when the family sits down to eat, that's the word. It means to life. And the word for life starts with a sound you make at the back of your throat.

You met l'chaim in year three, raised at tables after mourning; today, the letter inside it. First, its look. Chet is a cousin of heh, the breath letter. Heh has a small gap at the top left, as if air can still slip out. Chet closes the gap: two legs and a roof, sealed. The sound changes too: not an easy h, but breath pushed against the back of the throat, ch. Second, the word. Put chet beside a yud, a tiny hanging stroke, and you have chai: alive, living. Its plural, chayim, is the everyday word for life. L'chaim simply means to life. Third, a sentence that gives the word weight. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses lays out the choice before the people. In the King James: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." Not just enjoy it. Choose it, as if life were something you keep picking up, day after day. Fourth, a custom. Tradition gives each Hebrew letter a number, and says chet and yud together add up to eighteen. So some people give gifts in multiples of eighteen, and some wear chai on a chain around their neck. And l'chaim isn't only for weddings. Over coffee with a friend you haven't seen in a while, it's a way of noticing, out loud, that you're both still here.

Lift the cup a little toward it, say l'chaim under your breath, and sip slowly; if you pray, give thanks for it.

1337.title: Tet
1337.hook: the first tet in the Torah is in tov, good (Genesis 1:4)
1337.howItsDone: The first chapter of Genesis, with its refrain that God saw it was good, is read in synagogue at the start of each yearly cycle of Torah readings; some teachers of the alef-bet introduce tet with the word tov.

segments.voice: Yesterday, glasses raised and one word: l'chaim, to life. Your line: chet for life. Today ends the week, with a letter the rabbis were glad to dream about.

Deep in the Talmud, in a tractate mostly about damages, oxen and pits and broken fences, the rabbis pause for something unexpected: dreams. What does it mean to dream about a certain animal, a certain fruit, a certain letter of the alef-bet? Some answers are puzzling. One is beautiful. If you see the letter tet in a dream, they say, it's a good sign. And they give a reason that sends you back to the first page of the Torah, to the very first morning of the world.
screen: `DREAMS, IN A BOOK OF DAMAGES.` → `A LETTER IN A DREAM.` → `TET IS A GOOD SIGN.`

segments.voice: First, the first morning. God says let there be light, and there is light. In the King James: "And God saw the light, that it was good." The Hebrew for good is tov, and it begins with tet. In the Talmud, in tractate Bava Kamma, that's the whole argument: the first time the Torah uses a tet, it's in the word good, so a tet in your dream is good news. Second, the rest of the chapter. Good doesn't appear once and vanish. As the world is made, light, sea, land, plants, stars, animals, the chapter keeps stopping to say God saw it was good. And at the end, looking at everything at once: "and, behold, it was very good." Tet comes back like a refrain. Third, the week just past. Seven letters, seven pictures. Gimel, running after someone in need. Dalet, a door, opened quietly. Heh, a breath added to a name. Vav, a hook that joins. Zayin, remembering on purpose. Chet, a toast to life. And now tet, good. Side by side, the alef-bet starts to read like a way of living. Fourth, your own week. The text pauses over the light and names it good before the rest of creation is finished. Good can be noticed on the first morning of anything.
screen: `AND GOD SAW THE LIGHT.` · `TOV: GOOD, BEGINNING WITH TET.` · `GOOD, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `A WEEK OF LETTERS.` · then, large: `IT WAS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Look back over this week the way Genesis looks back over each day, and find one thing that was good: not perfect, good, like a meal, light through a window, a conversation that went better than expected. Hold it, say quietly to yourself, that was good, and if there's room, find one more; if you pray, give thanks for what you found.
Tet. The letter that begins tov, good, the word God says over the first light. Today's word.
Your line: tet for good. The rabbis even found it in dreams. Seven letters, one good week.
